claim: Transposable element (TE) activity is repressed in animal gonads by PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) produced by piRNA clusters.
source: Transposable element (TE) activity is repressed in animal gonads by PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) produced by piRNA clusters.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Current models in flies propose that germinal piRNA clusters are functionally defined by the maternal inheritance of piRNAs produced during the previous generation.
source: Current models in flies propose that germinal piRNA clusters are functionally defined by the maternal inheritance of piRNAs produced during the previous generation.
evidence: This statement references current models in the field.

claim: Raising flies at high temperature (29°C) instead of 25°C triggers the stable conversion of an inactive BX2 locus into actively producing functional piRNAs.
source: we show here that raising flies at high temperature (29°C) instead of 25°C triggers the stable conversion of this locus from inactive into actively producing functional piRNAs.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increase of antisense transcripts from the cluster at 29°C combined with the requirement of transcription of euchromatic homologous sequences suggests a role of double stranded RNA in the production of de novo piRNAs.
source: The increase of antisense transcripts from the cluster at 29°C combined with the requirement of transcription of euchromatic homologous sequences, suggests a role of double stranded RNA in the production of de novo piRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first case of the establishment of an active piRNA cluster by environmental changes in the absence of maternal inheritance of homologous piRNAs.
source: This report describes the first case of the establishment of an active piRNA cluster by environmental changes in the absence of maternal inheritance of homologous piRNAs.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: In humans, growing evidence has implicated TE in several disorders such as cancers defining a new field of diseases called transposopathies.
source: In humans, growing evidence has implicated TE in several disorders such as cancers defining a new field of diseases called transposopathies (Wylie et al., 2016a; Wylie et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other work.

claim: In the animal germline, TE activity is controlled at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels by small RNAs called piRNAs associated with the PIWI clade of germline Argonaute proteins (Piwi, Aub and Ago3 in Drosophila).
source: In the animal germline, TE activity is controlled at both transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels by small RNAs called piRNAs associated with the PIWI clade of germline Argonaute proteins (Piwi, Aub and Ago3 in Drosophila) (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007; Le Thomas et al., 2013; Sienski et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: piRNAs are processed from transcripts produced from specific heterochromatic loci enriched in TE fragments, called piRNA clusters.
source: piRNAs are processed from transcripts produced from specific heterochromatic loci enriched in TE fragments, called piRNA clusters (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: piRNA cluster loci undergo non-canonical transcription, ignoring splicing and transcription termination signals, licensed by specific protein complexes such as Rhino-Deadlock-Cutoff and Moonshiner-TRF2.
source: These loci undergo non-canonical transcription, ignoring splicing and transcription termination signals, licensed by specific protein complexes such as Rhino-Deadlock-Cutoff (Mohn et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014) and Moonshiner-TRF2 (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When a new TE inserts into a naive genome, it will freely transpose until one copy gets inserted into a piRNA cluster leading to the production of homologous new TE piRNAs that will then repress transposition.
source: Thus, when a new TE inserts into a naive genome, it will freely transpose until one copy gets inserted into a piRNA cluster leading to the production of homologous new TE piRNAs that will then repress transposition (Brennecke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a model supported by citation.

claim: Exogenous sequences inserted into preexisting piRNA clusters lead to the production of matching piRNAs.
source: In support of this idea, exogenous sequences inserted into preexisting piRNA clusters lead to the production of matching piRNAs (de Vanssay et al., 2012; Hermant et al., 2015; Marie et al., 2017; Muerdter et al., 2012; Pöyhönen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including the authors' own work.

claim: The specificity of the efficient repression mediated by piRNAs appears to be determined solely by the piRNA cluster sequences.
source: The specificity of the efficient repression mediated by piRNAs appears to be determined solely by the piRNA cluster sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: Histone H3 lysine nine tri-methylation (H3K9me3) that is recognized by Rhino, a paralog of heterochromatin protein HP1, is a shared feature of piRNA clusters.
source: Histone H3 lysine nine tri-methylation (H3K9me3) that is recognized by Rhino, a paralog of heterochromatin protein HP1 (Klattenhoff et al., 2009), is a shared feature of piRNA clusters.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Enrichment of H3K9me3 is not specific to piRNA clusters.
source: Enrichment of H3K9me3, however, is not specific to piRNA clusters
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tethering Rhino onto a transgene leads to the production of piRNAs only when both sense and antisense transcripts are produced.
source: tethering Rhino onto a transgene leads to the production of piRNAs only when both sense and antisense transcripts are produced (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claim: Neither H3K9me3 marks nor having Rhino-bound is sufficient to induce piRNA production.
source: This suggests that neither H3K9me3 marks nor having Rhino-bound is sufficient to induce piRNA production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study.

claim: One current model proposes that piRNAs clusters are defined and activated at each generation by the deposition in the egg of their corresponding piRNAs from the mother.
source: One current model proposes that piRNAs clusters are defined and activated at each generation by the deposition in the egg of their corresponding piRNAs from the mother (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a model from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The first case of a stable transgenerational epigenetic conversion known as paramutation in animals was previously described by the authors.
source: In support of this model, we previously described the first case of a stable transgenerational epigenetic conversion known as paramutation in animals (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: Paramutation is defined as an epigenetic interaction between two alleles of a locus, through which one allele induces a heritable modification of the other allele without modifying the DNA sequence.
source: This phenomenon was first described in plants and defined as "an epigenetic interaction between two alleles of a locus, through which one allele induces a heritable modification of the other allele without modifying the DNA sequence" (Brink, 1956; Chandler, 2007).
evidence: This is a definition from the literature supported by citations.

claim: An inactive non-producing piRNA cluster of P transgene insertions inherited from the father can be converted into a piRNA-producing cluster by piRNAs inherited from the mother.
source: In our previous study, we showed that an inactive non-producing piRNA cluster of P transgene insertions inherited from the father can be converted into a piRNA-producing cluster by piRNAs inherited from the mother (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: The BX2 cluster consists of seven P(lacW) transgenes resulting from multiple and successive P(lacW) transposition events.
source: To address this paradox, we used the same BX2 cluster of seven P(lacW) transgenes, which resulted from multiple and successive P(lacW) transposition events, thus resembling the structure of natural piRNA clusters (Dorer and Henikoff, 1994).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system supported by citation.

claim: The BX2 locus can exist in two epigenetic states for the production of germline piRNAs: the inactive state (BX2OFF) and the active state (BX2ON).
source: The key advantage of the BX2 locus is that it can exist in two epigenetic states for the production of germline piRNAs: 1) the inactive state (BX2OFF) does not produce any piRNAs and thus is unable to repress the expression of homologous sequences, and 2) the active state (BX2ON) produces abundant piRNAs that functionally repress a homologous reporter transgene in the female germline (de Vanssay et al., 2012; Hermant et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Flies in their natural habitat exhibit a temperature range from 25°C to 29°C, especially in the context of global warming.
source: It should be noted that flies in their natural habitat exhibit this range of temperature, especially in the context of global warming.
evidence: This is a statement about the natural environment of flies.

claim: Earlier studies of hybrid dysgenesis reported that high temperature enhances P-element repression.
source: Earlier studies of hybrid dysgenesis reported that high temperature enhances P-element repression (Ronsseray et al., 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to earlier work.

claim: Thermic modification of P repression can persist over several generations.
source: and that thermic modification of P repression can persist over several generations (Ronsseray, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to earlier work.

claim: P-element repression in a strain carrying two P-elements inserted into a subtelomeric piRNA cluster can be stimulated by heat treatment.
source: Moreover, P-element repression in a strain carrying two P-elements inserted into a subtelomeric piRNA cluster can be stimulated by heat treatment (Ronsseray et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citation to earlier work.

claim: The tracking of natural invasion of P elements in Drosophila simulans confirmed the key role of high temperature in the establishment of repression through generations.
source: Very recently, the tracking of natural invasion of P elements in Drosophila simulans confirmed the key role of high temperature in the establishment of repression through generations (Kofler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: At 25°C BX2OFF does not synthesize functional piRNAs complementary to P(TARGET)GS resulting in ß-Galactosidase expression in whole ovaries.
source: As was previously described (de Vanssay et al., 2012), at 25°C BX2OFF does not synthesize functional piRNAs complementary to P(TARGET)GS resulting in ß-Galactosidase expression in whole ovaries of BX2OFF, P(TARGET)GS lines (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines, functional lacZ piRNAs are synthesized in the germline where they specifically repress the P(TARGET)GS ß-Galactosidase expression.
source: Whereas in BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines, functional lacZ piRNAs are synthesized in the germline where they specifically repress the P(TARGET)GS ß-Galactosidase expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both BX2OFF, P(TARGET)GS and BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines incubated at 25°C for 23 generations maintained their epigenetic state.
source: Both BX2OFF, P(TARGET)GS and BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines incubated at 25°C for 23 generations maintained their epigenetic state, showing that both epialleles are stable (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: At 29°C, the repression capacity of BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines remained stable through 25 generations.
source: At 29°C, the repression capacity of BX2ON, P(TARGET)GS lines remained stable through 25 generations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Among the BX2OFF, P(TARGET)GS lines at 29°C, 24.7% of females analyzed during 25 generations showed a complete and specific germline ß-Galactosidase repression.
source: Among the BX2OFF, P(TARGET)GS lines, 24.7% of females analyzed during 25 generations showed a complete and specific germline ß-Galactosidase repression (n = 3812, Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The appearance of females showing ß-Galactosidase repression at 29°C was gradual and stochastic, resulting in a global frequency that increased with the number of generations.
source: Interestingly, the appearance of females showing ß-Galactosidase repression was gradual and stochastic, resulting in a global frequency that increased with the number of generations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The silencing capacities of the BX2ON epiallele induced at 29°C remained stable during 50 additional generations at 25°C.
source: In all cases, the silencing capacities of the BX2ON epiallele induced at 29°C remained stable during 50 additional generations at 25°C (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Maternal inheritance of either BX2Θ or BX2* loci leads to complete and stable repression of ß-Galactosidase expression.
source: Maternal inheritance of either BX2Θ or BX2* loci leads to complete and stable repression of ß-Galactosidase expression (n flies = 152 and 159, respectively, Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Paternal inheritance of either BX2Θ or BX2* loci results in ß-Galactosidase expression, and thus a definitive loss of BX2 silencing capacities.
source: whereas paternal inheritance of either BX2Θ or BX2* loci, that is in absence of maternal piRNA deposition, results in ß-Galactosidase expression, and thus a definitive loss of BX2 silencing capacities (n flies = 156 and 155, respectively, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Progeny with a paternally inherited BX2OFF locus and maternally inherited BX2* piRNAs, but lacking the maternally BX2* genomic locus, have 100% conversion.
source: Secondly, we previously showed that progeny with a paternally inherited BX2OFF locus and maternally inherited BX2* piRNAs, but lacking the maternally BX2* genomic locus, have 100% conversion (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: BX2Θ is paramutagenic, showing 100% of repression capacity over 20 generations.
source: Silencing measured over 20 generations revealed 100% of repression capacity showing that BX2Θ is also paramutagenic (n flies = 159, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Unique reads matching the P(lacW) sequences were identified only in the BX2Θ and BX2* libraries.
source: Unique reads matching the P(lacW) sequences were identified only in the BX2Θ and BX2* libraries (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most small RNAs from BX2Θ and BX2* display all of the characteristics of bona fide germline piRNAs.
source: Most of these small RNAs display all of the characteristics of bona fide germline piRNAs, that is a high proportion of 23–29 nt with a strong U bias on the first 5' nucleotide, an enrichment of a 10 nucleotide overlap between sense and antisense piRNAs, also known as the ping-pong signature, and a high proportion of reads with A at the tenth position among the 10 nt overlapped reads (Figure 2B–C) (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C and citations to established characteristics of piRNAs.

claim: The 42AB piRNA cluster presented no significant difference between the three genotypes (BX2OFF, BX2Θ, BX2*).
source: As a control, the 42AB piRNA cluster, a canonical germline dual-strand piRNA cluster, presented no significant difference between the three genotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High temperature can initiate piRNA production from BX2 naive sequences (BX2OFF).
source: Therefore, these results show that high temperature can initiate piRNA production from BX2 naive sequences (BX2OFF)
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Once a piRNA cluster is activated for piRNA production, the 'ON' state is maintained at each generation by maternal inheritance of piRNAs.
source: and strongly suggest that once a piRNA cluster is activated for piRNA production, the 'ON' state is maintained at each generation by maternal inheritance of piRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In both BX2Θ and BX2* strains, H3K9me3 and Rhino were similarly enriched over the P(lacW) transgene compared to the BX2OFF strain.
source: In both strains BX2Θ and BX2*, H3K9me3 and Rhino were similarly enriched over the P(lacW) transgene compared to the BX2OFF strain, significantly for H3K9me3 (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: De novo activation of BX2OFF by 29°C treatment (BX2Θ) or paramutation by maternal inheritance of homologous piRNAs (BX2*) lines leads to similar functional and molecular properties.
source: Taken together, these results show that de novo activation of BX2OFF by 29°C treatment (BX2Θ) or paramutation by maternal inheritance of homologous piRNAs (BX2*) lines leads to similar functional and molecular properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Epigenetic conversion of BX2OFF into BX2Θ is an instantaneous and complete event occurring at a low frequency per egg chamber and at each generation that is kept at 29°C.
source: These results support our hypothesis whereby epigenetic conversion of BX2OFF into BX2Θ is an instantaneous and complete event occurring at a low frequency per egg chamber and at each generation that is kept at 29°C.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Environmental modifications like high temperature experienced during one generation might stably modify the epigenome of the future ones.
source: Altogether, our results illustrate how environmental modifications like high temperature experienced during one generation might stably modify the epigenome of the future ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: A newly acquired epigenetic state may spread in a given population within a few generations.
source: Such a newly acquired epigenetic state may spread in a given population within a few generations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: BX2OFF and BX2ON produce similar amounts of sense and antisense transcripts.
source: Previously, we showed that BX2OFF and BX2ON produce similar amounts of sense and antisense transcripts (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: BX2OFF transcripts do not lead to ß-Galactosidase expression in the germline nor piRNA production.
source: However, these transcripts do not lead to ß-Galactosidase expression in the germline nor piRNA production in the BX2OFF line.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous observations.

claim: There is a significant increase in the steady-state BX2 RNA levels at 29°C compared to 25°C.
source: We observed a significant increase in the steady-state BX2 RNA levels at 29°C compared to 25°C (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only BX2 antisense transcripts, corresponding to antisense lacZ transcripts, increase at 29°C.
source: Remarkably, strand-specific qRT-PCR experiments revealed that only BX2 antisense transcripts, corresponding to antisense lacZ transcripts, increase at 29°C (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by strand-specific RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BX2 is inserted into the AGO1 gene in a convergent transcription manner.
source: As BX2 is inserted into the AGO1 gene in a convergent transcription manner (de Vanssay et al., 2012), Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous work and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AGO1 transcript isoforms that are initiated upstream the BX2 insertion point are significantly increased at 29°C.
source: AGO1 transcript isoforms that are initiated upstream the BX2 insertion point are significantly increased at 29°C (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: At 29°C, an increase of transcription from the AGO1 promoters located upstream the BX2 insertion point could lead to an increase of BX2 antisense RNA transcription.
source: Thus, it is possible that, at 29°C, an increase of transcription from the AGO1 promoters located upstream the BX2 insertion point could lead to an increase of BX2 antisense RNA transcription.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: The amount of P(TARGET)GS transcripts is decreased at 29°C compared to 25°C.
source: Interestingly, the amount of P(TARGET)GS transcripts is affected by temperature but in the opposite way to BX2, as less transcripts were measured at 29°C compared to 25°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No piRNAs were produced from the BX2 locus at 25°C nor after one generation at 29°C.
source: Strikingly, no piRNAs were produced from the BX2 locus at 25°C nor after one generation at 29°C.
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data.

claim: The increase of BX2 antisense transcripts observed at 29°C did not correlate with an increase of corresponding antisense piRNAs.
source: Thus, the increase of BX2 antisense transcripts observed at 29°C (Figure 4B) did not correlate with an increase of corresponding antisense piRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: At 25°C and 29°C, BX2OFF produced the same low amount of 21 nt small RNAs, equally distributed between sense and antisense.
source: At 25°C and 29°C, BX2OFF produced the same low amount of 21 nt small RNAs, equally distributed between sense and antisense (Figure 4G,H,I)
evidence: This is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4G,H,I.

claim: BX2 transcripts are processed into siRNAs.
source: suggesting that BX2 transcripts are processed into siRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size of the small RNAs.

claim: At 29°C, AGO1 is still not producing small RNAs.
source: and showed that, at 29°C, AGO1 is still not producing small RNAs (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: 21 nt small RNA production was restricted to BX2 sequences.
source: These data indicate that 21 nt small RNA production was restricted to BX2 sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: In the absence of P(TARGET)GS, among 1137 G2 females analyzed, only one female presented partial repression of the ß-Galactosidase expression and none presented complete repression.
source: Among the 1137 G2 females analyzed, only one female presented partial repression of the ß-Galactosidase expression and none presented complete repression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in conversion frequency between BX2, P(TARGET)GS lines and BX2 lines without P(TARGET)GS was highly significant.
source: If we compare these results with those obtained with the BX2, P(TARGET)GS lines (Figure 3), the difference was highly significant (p=8.5×10−6, homogeneity χ2 = 23.35 with 2 degrees of freedom, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: After 30 generations at 29°C, no female showing ß-Galactosidase repression was observed in eight independent lines in which BX2 was recombined into the same genetic background but without the P(TARGET)GS transgene.
source: After 30 generations at 29°C, no female showing ß-Galactosidase repression was observed (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 9.

claim: A homogeneity χ2 test comparing repression occurrence in BX2, P(TARGET)GS lines and in recombined BX2 lines is highly significant, arguing against a background effect of the P(TARGET)GS line in the conversion phenomenon.
source: A homogeneity χ2 test comparing, at G13, the repression occurrence in BX2, P(TARGET)GS lines (31/161, Supplementary file 1) and in recombined BX2 lines (0/975, Supplementary file 9) is highly significant (p=7.04×10−44, homogeneity χ2 = 192.9 with 1 degree of freedom), arguing against a background effect of the P(TARGET)GS line in the conversion phenomenon.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of P(TARGET)G, BX2 was converted at 29°C at a rate comparable with that observed with P(TARGET)GS.
source: Additionally, we reproduced the experiment with an euchromatic P(TARGET) expressed only in the germline and referred to hereinafter as 'P(TARGET)G' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B). In the presence of P(TARGET)G, BX2 was converted at 29°C at a rate comparable with that observed with P(TARGET)GS (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 10.

claim: BX2 conversion by temperature cannot be attributed to any specificity linked to the P(TARGET)GS insertion.
source: These data show that BX2 conversion by temperature cannot be attributed to any specificity linked to the P(TARGET)GS insertion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: In the presence of P(TARGET)S (expressed only in somatic cells), BX2 was not converted at 29°C.
source: To know if the transcription of the P(TARGET)GS (or of the P(TARGET)G) is required, we reproduced the same experiment with another euchromatic transgene that is not expressed in the germline but in the somatic cells surrounding the germ cells and therefore referred to hereinafter as 'P(TARGET)S' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B). In the presence of P(TARGET)S, BX2 was not converted at 29°C (0/784, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The transcription of a reporter transgene sharing homologous sequences (i.e. lacZ) with BX2 is required in the germline for BX2 conversion at 29°C.
source: We conclude that the transcription of a reporter transgene sharing homologous sequences (i.e. lacZ) with BX2 is required in the germline for BX2 conversion at 29°C.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: In the absence of P(TARGET) sequences, at 29°C BX2OFF produces an elevated number of antisense transcripts, no piRNAs and is unable to be converted to BX2ON.
source: To summarize, in the absence of P(TARGET) sequences, at 29°C BX2OFF produces an elevated number of antisense transcripts, no piRNAs and is unable to be converted to BX2ON.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When a P(TARGET) is present and transcribed in the germline, BX2 conversion and piRNA production are observed at 29°C.
source: In contrast, when a P(TARGET) is present and transcribed in the germline, BX2 conversion and piRNA production are observed at 29°C.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: At 29°C, double strand RNA (dsRNA) made of the excess of BX2 antisense transcripts and the sense P(TARGET) transcripts could be a prerequisite for the production of de novo piRNAs and the conversion of BX2 into an active piRNA cluster.
source: Although much of the mechanistic aspects of BX2 conversion remain unknown, these findings lead us to propose that, at 29°C, double strand RNA (dsRNA) made of the excess of BX2 antisense transcripts and the sense P(TARGET) transcripts could be a prerequisite for the production of de novo piRNAs and the conversion of BX2 into an active piRNA cluster (see recapitulative model Figure 5).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: In Arabidopsis, increasing temperature induces transcriptional activation of repetitive elements.
source: In Arabidopsis for instance, increasing temperature induces transcriptional activation of repetitive elements (Ito et al., 2011; Pecinka et al., 2010; Tittel-Elmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work.

claim: In mutants for siRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis, high frequency of new TE insertions was observed in the progeny of stressed plants.
source: Whether these changes involve chromatin modifications is not clear but none of these modifications have been found to be heritable through generations except in mutants for siRNA biogenesis where high frequency of new TE insertions was observed in the progeny of stressed plants (Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: In animals, response to heat can result in modification of DNA methylation at specific loci in reef building coral, chicken and wild guinea pigs.
source: In animals, response to heat can result in modification of DNA methylation at specific loci in reef building coral (Dimond and Roberts, 2016), chicken (Yossifoff et al., 2008) and wild guinea pigs (Weyrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work.

claim: In wild guinea pigs, modifications affecting ≈50 genes are inherited in G1 progeny.
source: In the latter, modifications affecting ≈50 genes are inherited in G1 progeny (Weyrich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: In Drosophila, heat-shock treatment of 0–2 hr embryos for one hour at 37°C or subjecting flies to osmotic stress induce phosphorylation of dATF-2 and its release from heterochromatin.
source: In Drosophila, heat-shock treatment of 0–2 hr embryos for one hour at 37°C or subjecting flies to osmotic stress induce phosphorylation of dATF-2 and its release from heterochromatin (Seong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: The defective chromatin state induced by heat-shock or osmotic stress is maintained for several generations before returning to the original state.
source: This defective chromatin state is maintained for several generations before returning to the original state.
evidence: This is based on the cited work.

claim: Neither heat-shock nor osmotic stress induces BX2 conversion.
source: We have tested if such stresses were able to convert BX2OFF into BX2ON in one generation but neither heat-shock nor osmotic stress induces BX2 conversion (Supplementary file 11)
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 11.

claim: BX2 activation does not depend on dATF-2.
source: suggesting that BX2 activation does not depend on dATF-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Fast et al. found less piRNAs at 29°C than at 18°C.
source: In a more recent paper, Fast et al. (Fast et al., 2017) found less piRNAs at 29°C than at 18°C.
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: RNAseq analyses of differentially expressed genes involved in the piRNA pathway were not conclusive, as some piRNA genes were more expressed at 29°C while others were less expressed as compared to the levels at 18°C.
source: However, RNAseq analyses of differentially expressed genes involved in the piRNA pathway were not conclusive, as some piRNA genes (ago3, aub, zuc, armi) were more expressed at 29°C while others (shu, hsp83, Yb) were less expressed as compared to the levels at 18°C (Fast et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the cited work.

claim: The enhancement of the piRNA ping-pong amplification loop observed at 29°C was attributed to RNA secondary structures.
source: Overall, the enhancement of the piRNA ping-pong amplification loop observed at 29°C was attributed to RNA secondary structures, because of a lack of specificity for any particular class of TE (Fast et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the cited work.

claim: In contrast to the authors' RT-qPCR results obtained at 25°C and 29°C, AGO1 was not differentially expressed between 18°C and 29°C in the Fast et al. study.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to our RT-qPCR results obtained at 25°C and 29°C (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), AGO1 was not differentially expressed between 18°C and 29°C (Fast et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison between the authors' data and the cited work.

claim: The difference in AGO1 expression can be explained because the authors checked for specific spliced transcripts of AGO1 (RA, RC and RD) that originate upstream the BX2 insertion point.
source: This difference can be explained, because, in our experiments, we checked for specific spliced transcripts of AGO1 (RA, RC and RD) that originate upstream the BX2 insertion point (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the experimental design.

claim: No statistical difference in the global amount of AGO1 transcripts between 25°C and 29°C is observed using primers located downstream the BX2 insertion point.
source: In agreement with Fast et al., no statistical difference in the global amount of AGO1 transcripts between 25°C and 29°C is observed using primers located downstream the BX2 insertion point (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The AGO1 promoter located downstream the BX2 insertion point, and responsible for the production of the RB isoform, is not sensitive to temperature.
source: This suggests that the AGO1 promoter located downstream the BX2 insertion point, and responsible for the production of the RB isoform (see Figure 4), is not sensitive to temperature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: Temperature modification might induce epigenetic changes in several species but the underlying mechanisms remain largely unsolved.
source: Taken together, these observations show that temperature modification might induce epigenetic changes in several species but the underlying mechanisms remain largely unsolved.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the literature review.

claim: Whole genome comparison of small RNA sequencing between BX2OFF and newly BX2ON heat-converted flies (BX2Θ) did not reveal additional regions stably converted for piRNA production.
source: Whole genome comparison of small RNA sequencing between BX2OFF and newly BX2ON heat-converted flies (BX2Θ) did not reveal additional regions stably converted for piRNA production (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No other loci are metastable for piRNA production, suggesting that all potential piRNA clusters are already active at 25°C.
source: This suggests that no other loci are metastable for piRNA production, that is all potential piRNA clusters are already active at 25°C.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: The BX2 locus is the result of successive induced transpositions of P(lacW) used to screen for white-variegating phenotype.
source: The BX2 locus is the result of successive induced transpositions of P(lacW) used to screen for white-variegating phenotype (Dorer and Henikoff, 1994).
evidence: This is based on the cited work.

claim: BX2 resembles natural TE clusters where TEs have the capacity to transpose into each other assembling structures named nested TE.
source: Thus, BX2 resembles natural TE clusters where TEs have the capacity to transpose into each other assembling structures named nested TE, as described in numerous genomes (Gao et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2007; Zanni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work.

claim: Some nested TE loci might have the capacity to be activated and respond to a new TE invasion.
source: Some nested TE loci might have the capacity to be activated and respond to a new TE invasion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: BX2-like tandemly inserted transgenes were shown to be new sites of HP1 enrichment in larval salivary glands, emphasizing a heterochromatic structure at the BX2 locus in somatic cells.
source: In Drosophila, BX2-like tandemly inserted transgenes were shown to be new sites of HP1 enrichment in larval salivary glands, emphasizing a heterochromatic structure at the BX2 locus in somatic cells (Fanti et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: BX2-like tandemly inserted transgenes cause pairing-dependent silencing.
source: and to cause pairing-dependent silencing (Dorer and Henikoff, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: When tested for repressing capacities, the BX2 strain is inactive for BX2 piRNA production.
source: When tested for repressing capacities, however, this strain is inactive for BX2 piRNA production (de Vanssay et al., 2012; Josse et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Maternally inherited P(lacW) piRNAs are able to paramutate with complete and stable penetrance from an inactive BX2 locus into an active locus for piRNA production.
source: We have shown that maternally inherited P(lacW) piRNAs are able to paramutate with complete and stable penetrance from an inactive BX2 locus into an active locus for piRNA production (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous work.

claim: The paramutated BX2 locus appeared to be a genuine piRNA cluster since it is sensitive to a number of factors known to be involved in piRNA biogenesis such as aub, rhi, cuff, zuc and moonshiner.
source: The paramutated BX2 locus appeared to be a genuine piRNA cluster since it is sensitive to a number of factors known to be involved in piRNA biogenesis such as aub, rhi, cuff, zuc (Hermant et al., 2015) and moonshiner (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number of transgene copies appears to be crucial in the process since smaller number of transgenes results in less somatic heterochromatinization, less pairing-dependent silencing and unstable paramutation.
source: The number of transgene copies appears to be crucial in the process since smaller number of transgenes results in less somatic heterochromatinization (Dorer and Henikoff, 1994; Fanti et al., 1998), less pairing-dependent silencing (Dorer and Henikoff, 1997) and unstable paramutation (de Vanssay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other work.

claim: The heterochromatic structure of a cluster precedes piRNA production.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the heterochromatic structure of a cluster precedes piRNA production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and literature.

claim: H3K9me3 levels on BX2OFF are slightly below the H3K9me3 level of piRNA producing states (BX2ON and BX2Θ).
source: This is supported by our ChIP experiments showing that H3K9me3 levels on BX2OFF are slightly below the H3K9me3 level of piRNA producing states (BX2ON and BX2Θ, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Rhino may be already present on the BX2OFF locus but below the threshold required for piRNA production.
source: The same observation can be made for Rhino (Figure 2E), suggesting that Rhino may be already present on the BX2OFF locus but below the threshold required for piRNA production as suggested by Akulenko et al. (2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP data shown in Figure 2E and a cited work.

claim: A locus made of repeated sequences and being likely heterochromatic (H3K9me3, Rhino) is a necessary but not sufficient condition to specify an active piRNA cluster.
source: Thus, a locus made of repeated sequences and being likely heterochromatic (H3K9me3, Rhino) is a necessary but not sufficient condition to specify an active piRNA cluster.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and literature.

claim: In the germline, piRNA clusters produce piRNAs from both strands.
source: In the germline, piRNA clusters produce piRNAs from both strands
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: In most cases, transcription initiates within clusters on both strands through the interaction of Rhino and Moonshiner.
source: and it was recently shown that, in most cases, transcription initiates within clusters on both strands through the interaction of Rhino and Moonshiner (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: In few cases, piRNA cluster transcription may take advantage of the read-through from a flanking promoter.
source: In few cases, however, piRNA cluster transcription may take advantage of the read-through from a flanking promoter (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Tethering Rhino onto a transgene leads to its repression but the production of piRNA depends on the presence of another transgene producing antisense RNA.
source: Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2014) have shown that tethering Rhino onto a transgene leads to its repression but the production of piRNA depends on the presence of another transgene producing antisense RNA.
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: In the context of the Pld promoter deletion, a gene flanking the 42AB piRNA cluster, flies can produce Pld piRNAs only if a Pld cDNA is expressed in trans.
source: Moreover, in the context of the Pld promoter deletion, a gene flanking the 42AB piRNA cluster, flies can produce Pld piRNAs only if a Pld cDNA is expressed in trans (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to other work.

claim: A model emerges predicting that simultaneous production of sense and antisense RNA is a shared requirement for piRNA production.
source: From all of these observations, a model emerges predicting that simultaneous production of sense and antisense RNA is a shared requirement for piRNA production.
evidence: This is a model based on the literature.

claim: Even if BX2OFF is transcribed on both strands, without additional signals, it still remains inactive for piRNA production.
source: However, even if BX2OFF is transcribed on both strands, without additional signals, it still remains inactive for piRNA production.
evidence: This is based on the authors' observations.

claim: The production of de novo piRNAs from BX2 requires a triggering signal.
source: In addition to having a number of heterochromatic repeats and a double stranded transcription, the production of de novo piRNAs from BX2 requires a triggering signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: BX2 conversion relies on the simultaneous increase of both sense and antisense RNAs.
source: From our experiments, BX2 conversion relies on the simultaneous increase of both sense and antisense RNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: An active role of euchromatic copies in the establishment of new piRNA clusters by high temperature appears to be consistent with what would naturally happen during the invasion of a naive genome by new TEs or when chromosomal breakages occur leading to the loss of piRNA cluster loci.
source: An active role of euchromatic copies in the establishment of new piRNA clusters by high temperature appears to be consistent with what would naturally happen during the invasion of a naive genome by new TEs or when chromosomal breakages occur leading to the loss of piRNA cluster loci (Asif-Laidin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings and cited work.

claim: At first, uncontrolled euchromatic TE transposition takes place before the establishment of repression.
source: At first, uncontrolled euchromatic TE transposition takes place before the establishment of repression.
evidence: This is a description of a natural process.

claim: Repression would occur after a copy integrates into a preexisting piRNA cluster or by the generation of a new cluster made by successive insertion of nested copies.
source: Such repression would occur after a copy integrates into a preexisting piRNA cluster or by the generation of a new cluster made by successive insertion of nested copies.
evidence: This is a description of a natural process.

claim: Clusters of elements cannot exist without transcriptionally active euchromatic copies.
source: Consequently, clusters of elements cannot exist without transcriptionally active euchromatic copies.
evidence: This is a logical inference.

claim: The increase of germline antisense transcripts upon stress or environmental factors, depending on the neighboring genomic environment, and the concomitant presence of numerous sense transcripts from euchromatic active copies, appear to be the starting signals for new piRNA production.
source: The increase of germline antisense transcripts upon stress or environmental factors, depending on the neighboring genomic environment, and the concomitant presence of numerous sense transcripts from euchromatic active copies, appear to be the starting signals for new piRNA production.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: These piRNAs can then be inherited at the next generation where they will stably paramutate the corresponding DNA locus with repetitive nature.
source: These piRNAs can then be inherited at the next generation where they will stably paramutate the corresponding DNA locus with repetitive nature.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: At that time, the triggering signal is no longer necessary since BX2 remains activated once flies get back at 25°C.
source: At that time, the triggering signal is no longer necessary since BX2 remains activated once flies get back at 25°C.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observation that converted BX2 remains stable at 25°C.

claim: Future generations remember what was once considered a threat only through the legacy of maternal piRNAs.
source: Future generations thus remember what was once considered a threat only through the legacy of maternal piRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.
